why-team-away-days-fade.title: Why team away days fade by Wednesday
why-team-away-days-fade.excerpt: The energy of an away day rarely survives the first full inbox. Here is how to make it last.
body: Most teams come back from an away day feeling closer and clearer. By the following Wednesday, most of that has gone. The problem is rarely the day itself.
What fades is anything that was not turned into a habit. Agreements written on flipcharts need an owner, a date and a place they will be seen again.
Before your next away day, decide which one or two rituals you want the team to keep, and plan the first three repetitions before anyone leaves the room.

feedback-is-a-skill.title: Feedback is a skill, not a personality trait
feedback-is-a-skill.excerpt: Good feedback givers are made, not born. Three habits that make the difference.
body: We often describe people as naturally good at feedback. In our experience, the people who are good at it have simply practised more.
Three habits make the biggest difference: describe behaviour rather than character, explain the impact, and ask what the other person sees.
Practise these in low-stakes conversations first so they are available when it matters.

wellbeing-starts-with-workload.title: Well-being starts with workload
wellbeing-starts-with-workload.excerpt: Resilience training cannot fix a job that does not fit in the week.
body: Well-being programmes often focus on helping people cope. That matters, but it is only half the picture.
If a role reliably needs fifty hours a week, the most effective well-being intervention is a conversation about priorities, not a breathing exercise.
Start with a simple workload review in each team and act on what you find.

naming-emotions-at-work.title: The surprising power of naming emotions at work
naming-emotions-at-work.excerpt: Putting a feeling into words takes some of its heat away. Here is how to use that.
body: Research on affect labelling suggests that naming a feeling can reduce its intensity. At work, that gives us a simple, practical tool.
Try adding a feelings check to the start of difficult meetings. One word each is enough.
Over time the team builds a shared vocabulary that makes hard conversations easier.
